title: Baked Tofu Lettuce Wraps
subtitle: with peanut sauce
menu_blurb: Baked tofu, mushrooms and water chestnuts tossed in a rich hoisin sauce, spooned into crisp butterhead lettuce cups and topped with carrot and crushed peanuts.
intro: A fresh, light, crunchy and surprisingly flavorful dish: baked tofu tossed in a rich sauce and served inside crisp, cup-shaped lettuce leaves. Great as an appetizer or a main dish.
origin: Lettuce wraps come from China, where they are known in Cantonese as san choy bow (“lettuce package”), and from across Southeast Asia, with traditional dishes like Thai miang kham and Laotian and Thai larb (meat salads served in leaf cups). They continue to be popular in restaurants as more people move toward lighter, lower-carb meals.

mise_en_place.label: Chop
mise_en_place.task: Tofu, mushrooms, water chestnuts and scallions

steps.title: Prepare
instructions: Chop the tofu, mushrooms and water chestnuts all the same size, about ¼ inch cubes.

steps.title: Make the sauce
instructions: In a small bowl, stir together the hoisin, soy sauce, rice vinegar, water and sesame oil. Set aside.

steps.title: Cook
instructions: Heat the avocado oil in a wok over medium-high heat.
Once the oil is hot, add the tofu and cook until it browns a little, about 5 to 8 minutes.
Add the mushrooms and keep cooking for another 4 minutes.
Stir in the water chestnuts, garlic, ginger, red pepper flakes and half the green onions. Cook for a few more minutes.
Pour the sauce over the mixture and stir to coat, adding a little more water as needed.

steps.title: Plate
instructions: Spoon the tofu mixture into the lettuce cups.
Garnish with the carrot, crushed peanuts and the rest of the green onions.

sauce.title: Peanut Sauce
sauce.method: Combine the sauce ingredients and mix briefly (it won’t come together right away), then microwave for 30 seconds. Mix again until smooth and set aside to cool. Adjust the sourness with vinegar, the saltiness with salt, and the spice to taste. Once cooled, thin with milk or water as needed.

items.name: Peanut butter, preferably smooth (crunchy is fine too)
Sweet soy sauce (kecap manis, thick like syrup)

tips.label: Flavor boost
tips.tip: Add more red pepper flakes to make it spicier.

tips.label: Substitution
tips.tip: Any kind of mushroom works, as long as you chop it small. Romaine works in place of butterhead lettuce, or serve the filling over rice.

tips.label: Meal prep hack
tips.tip: The filling keeps for a couple of days in the refrigerator, so it’s easy to make ahead for appetizers or a main meal.

notebook.question: What is tofu, and is it good for you?
answer: Yes, tofu is exceptionally good for you. It is a nutrient-dense, plant-based protein made from curdled soy milk pressed into blocks. It is a complete protein, containing all nine essential amino acids your body can’t make on its own, which makes it an excellent alternative to meat. It is high in iron and calcium, low in fat, cholesterol-free, and safe to eat every day.
Its nutrition varies mainly with firmness. Firmer varieties hold less water, so they carry more protein, fat, and calories per serving.

table.label: Baked
table.text: Pre-cooked, dense, exceptionally firm and chewy. The most protein, about 150 calories and 14 to 16 g protein per 100 g. Best sliced into sandwiches, tossed into salads, or in quick stir-fries.

table.label: Extra firm or firm
table.text: A solid block packed in water that holds its shape but needs pressing. About 90 calories and 9 to 10 g protein per 100 g. Best cubed for baking, pan-fried, grilled, or crumbled into a breakfast scramble.

table.label: Medium or soft
table.text: Delicate, smooth, and crumbles easily. About 70 calories and 7 g protein per 100 g. Best steamed whole, dropped into hot soups, or in mapo tofu.

table.label: Silken
table.text: Custard-like, smooth and glossy, and turns liquid when blended. About 55 calories and 5 g protein per 100 g. Best blended into creamy sauces, vegan desserts, smoothies, or as an egg substitute in baking.

benefits.label: Heart health
benefits.text: Cholesterol-free and low in saturated fat, tofu may help reduce LDL cholesterol. Studies show eating at least one serving a week may lower heart disease risk by 18%.

benefits.label: Nutrient-rich
benefits.text: A good source of iron, manganese, selenium, phosphorus, and calcium, especially when made with calcium sulfate.

benefits.label: Cancer risk reduction
benefits.text: Tofu contains isoflavones, which have antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties and potential protective effects against breast, prostate, and colorectal cancers.

benefits.label: Bone health
benefits.text: Its high calcium and magnesium content helps prevent osteoporosis.
